title: An ozone and moisture product gave no clear time-transfer gain for forest injury in four eastern US tests in 1994-2010
abstract: We tested whether an ozone and soil moisture product improves plant injury predictions in a different time period. We used a verified public-data panel from US Forest Service surveys, EPA ozone monitors and NOAA moisture fields. Four tests used two eastern US regions and transfers between 1994-2002 and 2003-2010. Models used the same monitored sites, visit-ending 60-day ozone, completed June-July moisture, visit date, plant and species counts, and a time trend. Adding the product changed Brier loss by +0.00260 and -0.00728 in the Northeast and +0.00579 and -0.00009 in North Central states. Positive values mean higher error. All four nominal family intervals included zero. Forward models also had higher loss than a constant training injury rate. Removing the time trend changed some results. This fixed model test did not establish a common gain or absence of an ozone mechanism. Small selected samples, coarse exposure, few test years, fixed training fits and unmeasured missed injury limit the result. Code, aggregate results and verified-source retrieval instructions are included.
